lines.text: AI researches in seconds but can invent facts, so today you learn to research like a careful journalist.
Perplexity, Gemini and ChatGPT’s search option look up the web and show links next to their answer.
These links are called sources or citations, and you can click them.
An answer without sources is only a starting idea, not a fact.
Click each link and find the exact sentence that supports the claim.
Check who wrote it, such as a government site, a known newspaper or a company report.
Also check the date, because rules, rates and deadlines change.
Watch for numbers with no source, dead links, sources that do not match the claim, and old dates.
These are signs of a hallucination or old information.
Remove the claim or find a better source.
Ask exactly the same question in two different AI tools.
If they agree and the sources check out, good.
If they disagree, go to the official source, like a ministry, regulator or the company itself, and trust that.
Perplexity is built for research, and it shows numbered sources next to the answer.
Ask for official websites, then click every number and find the exact sentence.
Check who published it and when, because an old page can be confidently wrong today.
Here a home baker asks about food-safety registration, and asks for official sources.
The first claim links to the official FSSAI website, which is a good sign.
But the renewal claim comes from a blog post from 2019, not from the official site.
Old or unofficial sources are a red flag, so we check the official website before using it.
We ask Gemini the same question and compare the two answers.
Both agree on FSSAI registration, but Gemini does not repeat the six-month claim.
When tools disagree, the official website decides, not the more confident answer.
Finally, we ask ChatGPT with search to fact-check our claims in a table.
One claim could not be verified, so it stays out of our note until we find proof.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
